name: Buddhist Philosophy

tagline.text: Suffering has causes, and seeing there is no lasting self can end it.

date_range: from c. 5th century BCE (the Buddha); in India to about the 11th century CE (late Yogācāra); living today
description: A tradition of argument that grew from the Buddha's teaching on how to end suffering. Later Indian thinkers built theories of the self, the mind and reality on it. The two main schools of Mahāyāna ('Great Vehicle') Buddhism in India were Madhyamaka, the 'Middle Way', and Yogācāra, 'yoga practice'.
debatable: Whether the Buddha himself was a philosopher is disputed. SEP presents him as the later Buddhist tradition understood him. This node covers only the Indian roots; Buddhism in Tibet, China and Japan is left out.

questions.text: If there is no lasting 'I', who is it that suffers, and who is reborn?
Why do I keep clinging to things that cannot last?

sources.section: b. The Four Noble Truths or Realities

questions.text: Do things exist on their own, or only in relation to other things and to my mind?

themes.title: Four truths about suffering
themes.text: The Buddha's core teaching is usually summed up in four truths. 'Suffering' here means more than pain. It is the frustration that comes from everything being impermanent. IEP notes the four are also 'realities' to practise, not a creed to believe.
items: There is a path that stops it.

sources.section: b. The Four Noble Truths or Realities

themes.title: No lasting self
themes.text: The Buddha taught non-self (anātman), at least as the later tradition read him. None of the parts that make up a person is a lasting 'I'. A person is a changing bundle of five kinds of physical and mental elements, the skandhas. None of them lasts, so none of them can be a self. Our sense of 'I' and 'mine' is the ignorance that causes suffering.

themes.title: The middle path
themes.text: The Buddha called his teaching a 'middle path' between two extremes. One extreme says persons are eternal. The other says they are wiped out at death. Both assume a real 'I'. Drop that, and the question of its fate never arises. Nāgārjuna's school, Madhyamaka, takes its name from this middle way.

themes.title: Emptiness
themes.text: Nāgārjuna taught that all things are 'empty' (śūnyatā). Empty of what? Of svabhāva: an existence of their own, independent of everything else. Things exist only by depending on other things, all the way down. Critics called this nihilism, the view that nothing exists. Nāgārjuna denied it.

sources.section: c. Ethics and the Charge of Nihilism

themes.title: Mind only
themes.text: The Yogācāra school put the mind first. Its signature teaching is 'mind only' (cittamātra): the world we perceive depends on being cognised by a mind. It also mapped eight kinds of consciousness, including a hidden 'store consciousness' that keeps the seeds of past actions. Scholars still debate how far this is idealism, the view that mind comes before matter.

sources.section: 2.2 The store or substratum consciousness and its functions

reacted_against.text: The ritual religion of the Brahmin priests, built on sacrifices set out in the Vedas, the ancient sacred texts. The late Vedic Upaniṣads shared this dissatisfaction with ritual. Many wandering seekers, the Buddha among them, also denied that the Vedas have the final word on the world.

links.label: a lasting self, denied and defended
links.reason: Buddhists rejected the unchanging self of the Upaniṣads (late Vedic texts) and the Vedas' authority. The Vedānta thinker Śaṅkara replied by rejecting Buddhist idealism and emptiness.

sources.quote: The Buddhists explicitly rejected any notion of an indivisible and unchanging self
rejected the authority of the Vedas
a stratum of (comparatively late) texts, the Upaniṣads
construes as the Madhyamika Buddhist, to be counter-intuitively nihilistic

thinkers.name: The Buddha
thinkers.summary: The Buddha is the founder of Buddhism; tradition calls him Gautama. 'Buddha' is a title meaning 'awakened'. He was born into the wealthy Śākya clan, near today's border between India and Nepal. The story is that he left home to seek an end to suffering. He reached enlightenment and taught for 45 years. His dates are disputed; many scholars now think he died around 405 BCE.

key_ideas.text: Suffering has causes, so removing the causes ends the suffering.
A person is a changing bundle of physical and mental elements, and no part is a lasting self (the later tradition's reading).
His teaching is a middle path between saying persons are eternal and saying they are wiped out at death.

study_prompt.text: Teach me the Buddha as a short Socratic module. Start with the founder of Buddhism, a man of the Śākya clan who flourished around 450 BCE and whose title means 'awakened', then the three key ideas: suffering has causes, so removing them ends it; no part of a person is a lasting self, as the later tradition read him; a middle path between eternal persons and being wiped out at death. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Nāgārjuna
thinkers.summary: Nāgārjuna was a Buddhist monk who lived some time between 150 and 250 CE, probably mainly in southern India. Little is known of his life. SEP calls him the most important Buddhist philosopher after the Buddha himself. His main work, the Fundamental Wisdom of the Middle Way, has 450 short verses.

key_ideas.text: All things are empty of svabhāva: none exists on its own, independent of everything else.
There is no bottom layer of reality on which everything else rests.
Emptiness is not nothingness: only because things depend on each other can suffering arise and end.

sources.section: c. Ethics and the Charge of Nihilism

study_prompt.text: Teach me Nāgārjuna as a short Socratic module. Start with the Buddhist monk of around 150–250 CE, probably from southern India, whom SEP calls the most important Buddhist philosopher after the Buddha, then the three key ideas: all things are empty of an existence of their own; there is no bottom layer of reality; emptiness is not nothingness, since only dependent things can arise and end. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

sources.section: c. Ethics and the Charge of Nihilism

thinkers.name: Asaṅga
thinkers.summary: Asaṅga and his (half-)brother Vasubandhu are credited with making Yogācāra a distinct school. Tradition says some of his works came from his teacher Maitreya, whom it identifies with the future Buddha. Which works are really his is still debated.

sources.section: 1.2 The main textual sources and figures of Yogācāra philosophy

key_ideas.text: His Compendium of Abhidharma explains the dharmas, the basic mental and physical building blocks of reality, from a Yogācāra view. Abhidharma is early Buddhism's careful, technical account of experience.

sources.section: 1.2 The main textual sources and figures of Yogācāra philosophy

key_ideas.text: His Summary of the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) is an influential overview of Yogācāra theory and practice.

sources.section: 1.2 The main textual sources and figures of Yogācāra philosophy

key_ideas.text: He and Vasubandhu set out and defended the key ideas of the Yogācāra scriptures in a sustained way.

sources.section: 1.2 The main textual sources and figures of Yogācāra philosophy

study_prompt.text: Teach me Asaṅga as a short Socratic module. Start with the 4th–5th-century Indian thinker who, with his brother Vasubandhu, made Yogācāra a distinct school, then the three key ideas: the Compendium of Abhidharma on the building blocks of reality; the Summary of the Great Vehicle on Yogācāra theory and practice; setting out and defending the key ideas of the Yogācāra scriptures. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

sources.section: 1.2 The main textual sources and figures of Yogācāra philosophy

thinkers.name: Vasubandhu
thinkers.summary: Vasubandhu was Asaṅga's (half-)brother and a co-founder of Yogācāra. His most famous book, the Treasury of Abhidharma, is not a Yogācāra work. It is a manual of Abhidharma, the earlier, technical Buddhist theory of experience. His Twenty Verses and Thirty Verses are core Yogācāra texts.

sources.section: 1.2 The main textual sources and figures of Yogācāra philosophy

key_ideas.text: His Twenty Verses defends the 'mind only' teaching against realists, who say objects exist outside the mind.

sources.section: 1.2 The main textual sources and figures of Yogācāra philosophy

key_ideas.text: No theory of objects built from atoms fits how we actually perceive the world.
The Buddha taught that outside objects exist only as a conventional teaching, not as ultimate truth.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Vasubandhu as a short Socratic module. Start with Asaṅga's brother, a 4th–5th-century co-founder of Yogācāra who also wrote a famous manual of earlier Buddhist theory, then the three key ideas: defending 'mind only' against realists; no atom-based theory of objects fits perception; the Buddha taught outside objects only as a conventional teaching. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

name: Vedānta

tagline.text: Hindu philosophy that reads the Upaniṣads as one teaching on self and ultimate reality.

date_range: Upaniṣads c. 700–300 BCE; Brahma Sūtra c. 200 BCE–200 CE; Śaṅkara (8th century CE) to Rāmānuja (11th–12th century CE); living today
description: A Hindu school that reads the Upaniṣads, ancient sacred texts, as one consistent philosophy. Its thinkers ask how the self relates to brahman, ultimate reality. Śaṅkara says they are one and the same. Rāmānuja says the self is real, but part of brahman.
debatable: IEP calls Vedānta only 'nominally' a school: it labels any attempt at a consistent reading of the Upaniṣads. The Upaniṣads are centuries older than the school itself. The 'dualist' branch of the later thinker Madhva (c. 1200 CE), for whom God and the self are not the same, has no card.

questions.text: Is my deepest self the same as the reality behind everything?
If reality is one, why do I see so many separate things?
Could knowing who I really am free me from suffering and rebirth?

sources.section: 3.4 Superimposition: The Fundamental Problem of Ignorance

themes.title: What is the self?
themes.text: The Upaniṣads are ancient Indian texts, composed between about 700 and 300 BCE. One of their great topics is the self, ātman. Uddālaka teaches his son that the self is an unseen essence in all living things, like salt dissolved in water. Yājñavalkya describes it as consciousness: the 'inner controller' behind all sensing and thinking.

themes.title: Self and ultimate reality
themes.text: Brahman means ultimate reality. Some Upaniṣad teachers, such as Śāṇḍilya and Yājñavalkya, say the self is brahman. Others, such as Uddālaka, never use the word. Are self and brahman fully identical, or is the self one aspect of brahman? Indian thinkers kept arguing over this, Vedānta most of all.

themes.title: Karma, rebirth and release
themes.text: Karma first meant ritual action. In the Upaniṣads it starts to stretch beyond ritual, toward moral cause and effect: you become good by good action. Later Upaniṣads name saṃsāra, the endless cycle of birth, death and rebirth. They also name mokṣa, release from that cycle, which Vedānta makes the goal.

themes.title: One without a second
themes.text: Advaita means 'non-dual'. Śaṅkara taught that the self is pure consciousness and identical with brahman. The many things we see are real only at the everyday level. At the ultimate level there is only brahman, as a rope mistaken for a snake was always only a rope.

themes.title: A self within God
themes.text: Rāmānuja's branch is called Viśiṣṭādvaita, 'qualified non-dualism'. For him brahman is a personal God: Vishnu, united with his consort Śrī. Individual selves are real and distinct. They belong to brahman as a body belongs to its soul. Devotion to God, bhakti, is the way to know brahman.

reacted_against.text: Ritual and sacrifice as life's highest aim: Vedānta puts knowledge and release first. Its early guide, the Brahma Sūtra, is a short explanation of the Upaniṣads' philosophy. It argued against the dualism of the rival Sāṃkhya school, which Śaṅkara also faulted for teaching many separate selves.

links.label: a lasting self, denied and defended
links.reason: Buddhists rejected the unchanging self of the Upaniṣads (late Vedic texts) and the Vedas' authority. The Vedānta thinker Śaṅkara replied by rejecting Buddhist idealism and emptiness.

thinkers.name: Uddālaka Āruṇi
thinkers.dates: teacher in the early Upaniṣads (texts c. 700–500 BCE)
thinkers.summary: Uddālaka Āruṇi is a brahmin (priestly) teacher in the early Upaniṣads. His best-known lesson, to his son Śvetaketu, is in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. He was Yājñavalkya's senior colleague and, by some accounts, his teacher. Śaṅkara later read his phrase 'you are that' as saying the self is brahman.

key_ideas.text: Things are not made from nothing: they grow out of one original being, as clay pots come from clay.
The self is an unseen essence spread through the body, like salt dissolved in water.
'You are that' (tat tvam asi): the self works in you the same way as in all living beings.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Uddālaka Āruṇi as a short Socratic module. Start with the brahmin teacher of the early Upaniṣads who instructs his son Śvetaketu in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, then the three key ideas: things grow out of one original being, as pots from clay; the self is an unseen essence, like salt in water; 'you are that': the self works the same way in all living beings. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Yājñavalkya
thinkers.dates: teacher in the early Upaniṣads (texts c. 700–500 BCE)
thinkers.summary: Yājñavalkya is the most prominent teacher in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, one of the oldest Upaniṣads. He debates other teachers, including Uddālaka, and instructs King Janaka. He describes the self as consciousness rather than as a life-giving essence.

key_ideas.text: The self is the 'inner controller' (antaryāmin), present in all sensing and thinking yet distinct from them.
The self can never be an object of thought, so ordinary language cannot describe it.
A person becomes good by good action and bad by bad action.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Yājñavalkya as a short Socratic module. Start with the most prominent teacher of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, who debates Uddālaka and teaches King Janaka, then the three key ideas: the self is the inner controller of sensing and thinking; the self can never be an object of thought or words; you become good by good action and bad by bad action. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Śaṅkara
thinkers.summary: Śaṅkara is the most authoritative philosopher of Advaita Vedānta. He flourished in the eighth century CE, though scholars dispute the exact dates. He saw himself as one teacher in a long line, a systematiser rather than a founder. He wrote the earliest surviving complete commentaries on three core texts. They are the Brahma Sūtra, an early explanation of the Upaniṣads, and the Bhagavad Gītā, which some schools count as an Upaniṣad. The third is ten main Upaniṣads.

key_ideas.text: Your true self is pure consciousness, one and the same as brahman.
Reality has two tiers: the everyday world, and the ultimate reality of brahman alone.
Ignorance makes us mistake the mind and body for the self; only knowing the self as brahman frees us.

sources.section: 3.4 Superimposition: The Fundamental Problem of Ignorance

study_prompt.text: Teach me Śaṅkara as a short Socratic module. Start with the eighth-century systematiser of Advaita Vedānta, who wrote the earliest surviving complete commentaries on its core texts, then the three key ideas: the true self is pure consciousness, identical with brahman; reality has an everyday tier and an ultimate tier; ignorance makes us mistake mind and body for the self, and self-knowledge frees us. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

sources.section: 3.4 Superimposition: The Fundamental Problem of Ignorance

thinkers.name: Rāmānuja
thinkers.summary: Rāmānuja was an eleventh-century philosopher from the Tamil-speaking south of India. He is the chief thinker of Viśiṣṭādvaita, one of Vedānta's three main forms. IEP calls him the first Indian philosopher to read the Vedas systematically as teaching a personal God.

sources.section: 8. Conclusion: Rāmānuja’s Place in the History of Indian Philosophy

key_ideas.text: Persons, qualities and objects are all real, yet all are united in brahman.
Brahman is the self of all, standing to us as a soul stands to its body.
Devotion (bhakti) is itself a kind of knowing, a direct seeing of brahman; theory alone does not free us.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Rāmānuja as a short Socratic module. Start with the South Indian philosopher of qualified non-dualism, the first to give the Vedas a systematic reading centred on a personal God, then the three key ideas: persons and things are real yet united in brahman; brahman stands to us as a soul to its body; devotion is itself a direct way of knowing brahman. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

name: Confucianism

tagline.text: Become good through ritual, family duty and study, and govern by example, not force.

date_range: 6th–3rd century BCE (Confucius, trad. 551–479 BCE, to Xunzi, died after 238 BCE)
description: The tradition that grew from Confucius's teaching in ancient China. It holds that ritual, family duty and study shape people into good 'gentlemen'. Rulers should lead by moral example, not force. Mencius and Xunzi later disagreed over whether human nature is good.
debatable: SEP avoids the word 'Confucian' because it is not well defined. The Chinese word usually translated 'Confucian', Ru, is older than Confucius and meant experts in ritual and music. SEP also stresses that what Confucius himself taught is still debated; this node follows the Analects. In 18th-century Europe, reports from Catholic Jesuit missionaries in China made him a sage of reason for Enlightenment writers. IEP counts that image among the myths that remade Confucius. Later Neo-Confucianism (Song period, 960–1279) is left out here.

questions.text: Is human nature good, or do we have to be shaped into goodness?
Can bowing, mourning and other rituals really make me a better person?

sources.section: 3. Modes of Moral Self-Cultivation: Ritual (li 禮) and Music (yue 樂)

questions.text: Should a leader guide people by example rather than by punishment?

themes.title: Ritual shapes the heart
themes.text: Ritual (li) first meant ceremonies, such as offerings to ancestors. Over time it came to cover etiquette and ethics in general. Confucius taught that performing ritual and music well reshapes your feelings. It limits greedy desires and prepares the ground for good character.

themes.title: The virtues of a gentleman
themes.text: The 'gentleman' (junzi) is the ideal person of the Analects, an early text of dialogues and stories about Confucius. By the Han period (202 BCE–220 CE), five of his virtues counted as a complete set:
items: benevolence: caring for others, seeing what is good from their point of view;
righteousness: refusing gain that breaks your values;
ritual propriety: playing each of your social roles well;
wisdom: judging people and situations rightly;
trustworthiness: being someone others can give responsibility to.

sources.section: 1. Confucius as Chinese Philosopher and Symbol of Traditional Culture

themes.title: Family first
themes.text: Filial piety (xiao) means respect and care for parents and elders. The Analects calls it 'the root of a person'. Confucius's disciple Youzi adds that someone filial at home rarely turns against superiors. A ruler boasted of a son who reported his father for stealing a sheep. Confucius replied that among his people, fathers and sons cover for each other.

themes.title: Governing by example
themes.text: Confucius thought rule by harsh rules and punishments makes people evasive and shameless. A ruler should guide people by ethical example instead, and use force only as a last resort. Mencius said that conquering the world through war is like 'climbing a tree in search of a fish'.

themes.title: Is human nature good?
themes.text: Mencius said human nature is good. Everyone has 'sprouts' of virtue, such as compassion, that grow with care. Xunzi said human nature is bad: following inborn desires leads to fighting and theft. For him goodness comes from 'artifice', the habits we build through ritual and teachers. Both agreed that anyone can become good.

reacted_against.text: Rule by force and strict punishment in a war-torn age. Also the Mohists, followers of Mozi, who called Confucian rituals wasteful and demanded equal care for everyone.

sources.section: 3. Modes of Moral Self-Cultivation: Ritual (li 禮) and Music (yue 樂)

links.reason: Daoism grew as a critical alternative to Confucius's followers, rejecting their human-made distinctions; Zhuangzi took aim at Mencius.

thinkers.name: Confucius
thinkers.summary: Confucius is a Latin form of Kongfuzi, 'Master Kong'. Tradition dates his life to 551–479 BCE. He was born in Zou, in today's Shandong Province, and held offices in the state of Lu. SEP calls him arguably the most significant thinker in East Asian history.

sources.section: 2. Sources for Confucius’s Life and Thought

key_ideas.text: Performing ritual and music well reshapes desires and starts moral growth.
Filial piety means real respect for parents, not just feeding them; it underpins good character and loyalty.
Learning and reflecting need each other: learning without reflecting leaves you lost.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Confucius as a short Socratic module. Start with 'Master Kong', traditionally dated 551–479 BCE, born in Zou and an office-holder in the state of Lu, then the three key ideas: ritual and music reshape desires; filial piety, real respect for parents, underpins good character and loyalty; learning and reflecting need each other. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

sources.section: 2. Sources for Confucius’s Life and Thought

thinkers.name: Mencius
thinkers.summary: Mencius is a Latin form of Mengzi, 'Master Meng'. He was born about a century after Confucius died, reportedly in the state of Zou. He travelled to persuade rulers to govern by benevolence, not brute force, and held office in the state of Qi. He is called the 'Second Sage', second only to Confucius.

key_ideas.text: Human nature is good: we all have 'sprouts' of benevolence, righteousness, wisdom and propriety.
His thought experiment of a child at a well aims to show that we are not purely selfish.
Caring for everyone equally, as the Mohists demand, goes against our nature, since we love our relatives more.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Mencius as a short Socratic module. Start with 'Master Meng', the 4th-century BCE 'Second Sage' who urged rulers to govern by benevolence, then the three key ideas: human nature is good, with sprouts of virtue; the child at the well shows we are not purely selfish; equal care for all goes against our nature. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Xunzi
thinkers.summary: Xunzi means 'Master Xun'; his name was Xun Kuang. He was probably born around 310 BCE and died some time after 238 BCE. For most of imperial Chinese history he was seen as a Confucian who went astray by rejecting Mencius. Only in recent decades has he been widely ranked among China's greatest thinkers.

key_ideas.text: Human nature is bad; what is good in us is 'artifice', built by our own effort.
Rituals and music, handed down by the ancient sages, train our emotions and hold society together.

sources.section: 3. Modes of Moral Self-Cultivation: Ritual (li 禮) and Music (yue 樂)

key_ideas.text: Heaven (tian) is the higher power behind the course of things; the Way (dao) is the right way to live. We cannot know Heaven, but we can know the Way, which the sages marked with rituals like signposts.

sources.section: 4. The Source of the Rituals: Heaven (tian 天) and the Way (dao 道)

study_prompt.text: Teach me Xunzi as a short Socratic module. Start with 'Master Xun', the 3rd-century BCE Confucian long seen as having gone astray by rejecting Mencius, then the three key ideas: human nature is bad and goodness is artifice; rituals and music train emotions and order society; we cannot know Heaven, but rituals mark the Way. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

name: Daoism

tagline.text: Follow the Way of nature: act without forcing, and see past human-made labels.

date_range: 5th–3rd century BCE (the Laozi and Zhuangzi texts); revived as 'Neo-Daoism' from the 3rd century CE; living today as a religion
description: A Chinese tradition built around the Dao, the 'Way' of nature. Its two classic books, the Laozi (also called the Daodejing) and the Zhuangzi, praise wu-wei (effortless action) and naturalness. They doubt that human-made labels of good and bad make life better.
debatable: The name 'Daoist school' was coined by a historian in the 2nd century BCE, after its classic books were written. 'Daoism' also names a later religion in which Laozi is a god. This node covers the philosophy. SEP and IEP stress that the two are deeply intertwined, and Daoists themselves rarely split them. Some modern scholars think Laozi never existed.

questions.text: What if trying harder is the problem, not the answer?
Do words like 'good' and 'bad' show how things are, or only how I see them?

sources.section: b. Chapter 2: Qi Wu Lun (Discussion on Smoothing Things Out)

questions.text: Could I live more freely by stepping outside the roles society hands me?

sources.section: a. Chapter 1: Xiao Yao You (Wandering Beyond)

themes.title: The Way
themes.text: Dao means a road or way. In Daoism it names the process of reality itself: how things come together while always changing. The Daodejing says we cannot fathom the Dao, because no name we give it can capture it.

themes.title: Effortless action
themes.text: Wu-wei (effortless action) is often translated 'non-action', but IEP says scholars generally agree that is wrong. It means acting naturally, without forcing or tampering. Zhuangzi tells of Ding the Butcher, who carves oxen so skilfully that he works by spirit, not by eye.

themes.title: Naturalness
themes.text: Ziran, literally 'self so', means naturalness or spontaneity. The Laozi says the Dao is not modelled on anything else. People should act in tune with the ways of nature. The sage is plain, like uncarved wood, and free of desires that society creates.

themes.title: Against human-made labels
themes.text: The Daodejing says human distinctions, in law, morals and beauty, create our troubles rather than solve them. IEP sums up the contrast with an image. Daoists want to stay like natural, unhewn wood; Confucians want to be carved and polished. Chapters 8–10 of the Zhuangzi make this criticism openly.

themes.title: Many points of view
themes.text: Zhuangzi's book is full of short, funny parables. Many ask whether our own point of view is the only one. Little birds laugh at the giant bird Peng, but their narrow view cannot take in his vast one. Zhuangzi admits we cannot be sure that what we fear, such as death, is bad. Whether he was a relativist, holding all views equal, is debated: SEP says yes, IEP doubts it.

sources.section: a. Chapter 1: Xiao Yao You (Wandering Beyond)
b. Chapter 2: Qi Wu Lun (Discussion on Smoothing Things Out)

reacted_against.text: The Confucian and Mohist debate about the right human way of life, with its moral training and fixed distinctions. Daoists looked instead to the natural Way.

thinkers.name: Laozi
thinkers.summary: Laozi means 'Old Master'. Chinese sources say he flourished in the sixth century BCE, as an older contemporary of Confucius. Some modern scholars think he is entirely legendary. The book named after him, the Laozi or Daodejing, was probably compiled from sayings over several centuries.

sources.section: 2. Date and Authorship of the Laozi

key_ideas.text: No name we give the Dao can capture it.
The sage practises wu-wei (effortless action), moving like a newborn, without plans or society's structures.
The best ruler stays in the background; when his work is done, the people say they are content.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Laozi as a short Socratic module. Start with the 'Old Master', traditionally of the sixth century BCE and possibly legendary, after whom the Daodejing is named, then the three key ideas: no name can capture the Dao; the sage acts effortlessly, like a newborn; the best ruler stays in the background. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Zhuangzi
thinkers.summary: Zhuangzi means 'Master Zhuang'; his personal name was Zhou. He flourished in the late fourth century BCE, around the time of Mencius. SEP calls him the pivotal figure of classical philosophical Daoism. The book Zhuangzi mixes his writing with others'. Chapters 1–7, the 'inner chapters', are most often ascribed to him.

key_ideas.text: 'Wandering beyond': step past your usual roles and values to see things more fully.

sources.section: a. Chapter 1: Xiao Yao You (Wandering Beyond)

key_ideas.text: We cannot be certain that what seems good for us, or bad, really is.

sources.section: b. Chapter 2: Qi Wu Lun (Discussion on Smoothing Things Out)

key_ideas.text: He doubts that 'sprouts' (inborn starts) of virtue can be told apart from weeds. SEP reads the line as aimed at Mencius.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Zhuangzi as a short Socratic module. Start with 'Master Zhuang', the late fourth-century BCE thinker whom SEP calls the pivotal figure of classical Daoism, then the three key ideas: wander beyond your usual roles and values; we cannot be sure what is really good or bad for us; his doubt that Mencius's sprouts of virtue can be told apart from weeds. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Wang Bi
thinkers.summary: Wang Bi was a leader of 'Learning in the Profound' (Xuanxue), a movement sometimes called Neo-Daoism. Despite his short life, he became a brilliant interpreter of the Laozi. His version of the Laozi became the standard text for almost 2,000 years. IEP notes that he was not himself a Daoist.

key_ideas.text: The Laozi is about the Dao as the source of being, not about long life or immortals.
Later writers credit him with the first extended treatment of 'principle' (li): the basic patterns governing the universe. This li is a different Chinese word from the Confucian li of ritual.

sources.section: 3. Modes of Moral Self-Cultivation: Ritual (li 禮) and Music (yue 樂)

key_ideas.text: Wu-wei (effortless action) means freedom from the dictates of desire, both in self-cultivation and in government.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Wang Bi as a short Socratic module. Start with the third-century leader of 'Learning in the Profound' whose version of the Laozi became the standard text, then the three key ideas: the Laozi is about the Dao as the source of being; what later writers praised as the first extended treatment of principle; wu-wei as freedom from the dictates of desire. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.
